extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (technology center examiners and SPEs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing a 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility analysis (Alice/Mayo two-step framework) for claims alleged to be directed to abstract ideas, including examiner tips, resources, and illustrative examples (Example 35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo framework (only analysis for 35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Alice/Mayo two-step framework as the only analysis when examining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Prior tests (e.g., Alappat special purpose computer test, Bilski machine-or-transformation as a stand-alone test, State Street UCT test) are no longer to be used as the governing analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the two-step flowchart (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: diamonds 2A and 2B). The Alice/Mayo framework incorporates principles from earlier cases but supersedes prior stand-alone tests. Eligibility should be considered for every claim, but claims that clearly do not seek to tie up an abstract idea need not be exhaustively analyzed using the framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1 is typically satisfied for process or product claims (e.g. a microprocessor can satisfy machine/manufacture). Claims that do not fall within a statutory category are usually intangible (e.g., signal per se, data per se, software per se). For more, see MPEP 2106(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — is the claim 'directed to' an abstract idea?
rubrics_metrics.description: After Step 1, determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea by comparing the claimed concept to concepts the courts have previously identified as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use court-identified abstract ideas as comparators. Be familiar with court cases in technologies similar to your art. The Abstract Idea Quick Reference Sheet (QRS) groups common abstract idea types and links cases; the Case Law Chart lists litigated patents by title and classification. Examiners are not required to rely on the most similar or the most recent case—any court case identifying a similar abstract idea may be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — evaluate whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, evaluate whether any additional element or combination of additional elements transforms the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., whether they provide 'significantly more' or an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations that may provide 'significantly more' include: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field; adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; and other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment. Considerations that may NOT provide 'significantly more' include: reciting a generic computer performing a generic computer function; words equivalent to 'apply the exception'; mere instructions to implement the judicial exception on a computer; insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering); generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use; and merely appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification as it would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim terms according to plain meaning unless the specification provides a special definition. When applying BRI, ask helpful questions: Does the method need to be performed by a computer or any particular device? What limits are imposed by the claim language on how information is obtained? How is the comparison accomplished? What is the result of a match (what happens when identity is verified)? These questions help define claim boundaries and whether elements are recited at a high level of generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the claim as a whole; consider all recited limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the claim in its entirety and consider all recited limitations in making the eligibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cherry-pick only certain elements—look at independent and relevant dependent claims and the specification. Also look beyond independent claims to other disclosed details that could be claimed in a manner that adds an inventive concept. The key inquiry: is the claim attempting to cover an abstract idea itself without significant limits on its application?

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate additional elements both separately and together to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual elements are conventional, their ordered combination can, in some cases (e.g., Diehr, BASCOM), add meaningful limits and result in an inventive concept. Consider how components and corresponding functions interact and whether they present a specific, discrete implementation that meaningfully limits the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware or machine limitations alone do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere presence of a machine (e.g., a processor, memory, or a 'particular' machine) or software in a claim does not automatically render it eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the Alice/Mayo framework is required—do not rely on the machine-or-transformation (Bilski) or special purpose computer (Alappat) tests as standalone reasons for eligibility. A generic processor performing generic functions, or merely adding conventional hardware, is not 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (mere data gathering) does not add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level steps of obtaining or gathering data, or other pre-solution/extra-solution activities that are conventional, typically do not add 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a step (e.g., 'obtaining data from a bank card') is recited at a high level of generality and covers known ways of obtaining data (mag stripe, RFID, microchip), courts treat it as mere data gathering, which is an insignificant extra-solution activity and will not meaningfully limit the abstract idea. Also consider whether the step represents well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use USPTO resources: Abstract Idea QRS and Case Law Chart
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Abstract Idea Quick Reference Sheet (QRS) and the Case Law Chart (available on the subject matter eligibility microsite) to identify common abstract idea types and relevant court cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QRS groups court cases within common types of abstract ideas for ease of reference. The Case Law Chart identifies litigated patents by title and classification. These resources are updated regularly; examiners should check for the most recent versions. The microsite URL and links are provided in training materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice compact prosecution—consider other statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: While determining eligibility, examiners should also fully examine claims under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, 112 and other related requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compact prosecution includes addressing utility, inventorship, double patenting, and non‑statutory double patenting along with 101. Point applicants to eligible subject matter in the specification when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, meaningfully integrated technical limitations can render claims eligible (Example-based guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting specific, detailed technical features and how they interact can add 'significantly more' to an abstract idea and render a claim eligible (illustrated by Example 35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Example 35, adding limitations such as generating a random code and transmitting it to a registered mobile device, a downloadable software module that generates an encrypted image including code data, reading/decrypting that image at the ATM, analyzing decrypted code data against the random code, or reciting a radio frequency reader and particular interactions between ATM and mobile device, were explained as adding significantly more. The training shows that these specific, discrete implementations present a practical application of fraud prevention and meaningfully limit the abstract idea, making the claim eligible at Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize yourself with abstract idea types common in your art
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the types of abstract ideas commonly encountered in your technology center/art unit will facilitate identifying whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea under Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being familiar with case law that addresses technologies similar to those your work group examines (and with the QRS and case law chart) will make the Step 2A comparison more straightforward and reliable.
